description: The 99 names of Allah, Tawhid, shirk, and what Islamic monotheism means for polytheism.
content_html:
Knowing Allah Through His Names

Muslims believe that Allah cannot be fully understood by human minds — He is infinite and beyond all created things. Yet Allah has made Himself known through His names and attributes. Islamic tradition speaks of the 99 names of Allah (Asma’ Allah al-Husna, meaning “the most beautiful names of Allah”). Each name reveals a facet of His nature, and reciting or meditating on these names is itself an act of worship. The opening chapter of the Qur’an, Surah al-Fatihah (Surah 1), begins with two of the most important names: Ar-Rahman (the Most Gracious, whose mercy extends universally to all creation) and Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful, whose particular mercy is reserved for believers).

Key Fact

Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim both come from the Arabic root meaning “mercy” but they are distinct: Ar-Rahman is universal mercy (extended to all of creation), while Ar-Rahim is particular mercy (given especially to believers who submit to Allah). Both names appear in the opening Basmala: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.”

Key Attributes of Allah

Among the 99 names, several are especially important for understanding the Islamic concept of God. Muslims affirm that Allah is:

  • Tawhid (Oneness) — the most fundamental attribute. Allah is utterly one, without partner, rival, or equal.
  • Omnipotent (Al-Qadir) — all-powerful. Surah al-Baqarah (2:117) declares: “Creator of the heavens and earth, when He decrees a matter, He only says to it: ‘Be,’ and it is.”
  • Benevolent — Allah is good and wills good for His creation. His mercy surpasses His justice.
  • Fair and Just (Al-‘Adl) — Allah judges every soul with absolute fairness; no injustice is possible from Him.
  • Transcendent — beyond and above all creation, entirely unlike anything in the universe. Surah al-Ikhlas (Surah 112) captures this: “Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent.”
  • Immanent — also present and close to creation. Surah Qaf (50:16) teaches: “We are closer to him than his jugular vein” — meaning Allah is intimately aware of and near to every human being.

Tawhid: The Heart of Islamic Belief

Tawhid is the cornerstone of the entire Islamic faith. It is not merely the belief that one God exists, but the conviction that Allah is uniquely, incomparably and indivisibly one — in His essence, His attributes and His actions. This principle cannot be compromised or diluted. Surah al-Ikhlas (Surah 112) is sometimes called “a third of the Qur’an” because it encapsulates this central truth so completely.

The implications of Tawhid are far-reaching. It means that Allah alone is worthy of worship. It means that no created thing — human, angelic, or natural — shares in His power or authority. It means that human beings are accountable directly to Allah and to no one else in ultimate terms. And it means that anything which threatens or contradicts Tawhid is the gravest possible error in Islam.

Shirk: The Opposite of Tawhid

Shirk means attributing partners, associates, or rivals to Allah. It is the direct opposite of Tawhid and is described in the Qur’an as the one unforgivable sin for someone who dies unrepentant. The Qur’an warns against the worship of polytheism in strong terms: Surah an-Najm (53:19-25) addresses the pagan practice of venerating goddesses alongside Allah, dismissing them as nothing more than human projections and names without divine reality.

From an Islamic perspective, polytheistic religions — whether ancient Greek or Roman religion, or any tradition that worships multiple distinct deities — commit shirk. This is not a matter of different cultures finding God in different ways; it is a fundamental theological error, because dividing divine power and worship among several beings contradicts the reality of Allah’s unique oneness.

Islam does not teach that polytheists are wicked people. Rather, it teaches that they have not yet arrived at the full truth about the nature of God. Islamic tradition holds that every human being is born with a natural inclination (the fitrah) towards recognising one God, and that polytheism represents a departure from this original knowledge through culture, tradition or error.

Tawhid and the Islamic View of Christianity

The doctrine of Tawhid has specific implications for how Muslims regard Christianity. While Muslims hold Jesus (Isa) in very high regard as a prophet and a word from Allah, the Christian belief in the Trinity — that God is one being in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit — is viewed in Islam as a form of shirk. Associating Jesus with Allah’s divine nature is seen as compromising Tawhid.

This is expressed clearly in Surah al-Ikhlas (Surah 112): “He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent.” The phrase “He neither begets” addresses directly the Christian affirmation that Jesus is the “Son of God” — a claim that, to Muslim understanding, implies a biological or ontological relationship that Allah cannot have with any creature.

Shi’a Muslims are careful to insist that their belief in the Imamate does not compromise Tawhid. The Imams are not divine; they do not share in Allah’s attributes or receive independent worship. Rather, they are considered perfectly righteous human beings who, by divine appointment, are the authoritative guides for the Muslim community and the trustworthy interpreters of the Qur’an.

Critics from the Sunni tradition have sometimes argued that the veneration shown to Imams — or to figures such as Hussayn at the Ashura commemoration — risks blurring the line between respect and worship, and therefore risks approaching shirk. Shi’a scholars reject this charge, arguing that reverence for holy people is categorically different from the worship (ibadah) that belongs to Allah alone.

Key Fact

Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is considered the most serious sin in Islam. It is the direct opposite of Tawhid. Surah al-Ikhlas (Surah 112) is the Qur’anic text most directly associated with expressing the absolute oneness and incomparability of Allah.
exam_tip_html: One of the most common errors on this topic is confusing Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim — examiners will expect you to distinguish them. Another frequent mistake is treating Tawhid as simply “belief in one God” without explaining what makes it distinctive: it is the absolute, undivided, incomparable oneness of Allah that rules out all association (shirk). For a 15-mark Discuss question on topics such as whether Islam and Christianity are more similar than different, you must show knowledge of why the Trinity is a theological problem from a Muslim perspective while also acknowledging that both traditions affirm one Creator God. Always cite a source: Surah 112 (al-Ikhlas) and Surah 50:16 (Qaf) are excellent choices. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of technical terms: ‘Tawhid’, ‘shirk’, ‘Ar-Rahman’, ‘Ar-Rahim’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 99 names of Allah describe His attributes; key examples include Ar-Rahman (universal mercy), Ar-Rahim (particular mercy for believers), Al-Qadir (omnipotent) and Al-‘Adl (just). Surah 112 (al-Ikhlas) and Surah 50:16 (Qaf) are the primary Qur’anic anchors for transcendence and immanence.
  • Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) is the foundational Islamic doctrine; shirk (associating partners with Allah) is its direct opposite and is considered the gravest sin. Both polytheism and the Christian Trinity are viewed by Muslims as forms of shirk.
  • The Shi’a Imamate does not compromise Tawhid in Shi’a theology because the Imams are respected human guides, not divine figures — though some Sunni scholars disagree about where veneration ends and worship begins.

practice_questions.marks: Shirk means associating partners with Allah / attributing partners, equals or associates to Allah. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Muslim belief in Tawhid.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: Tawhid is the belief in the absolute oneness of Allah (1 mark); this means Allah is unique, undivided, without partner or equal, and that He alone is worthy of worship (1 mark for development, e.g. linking to Surah 112 or explaining what this rules out). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim as names of Allah.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: both names derive from the Arabic root for mercy (1 mark); Ar-Rahman refers to Allah's universal mercy extended to all of creation (1 mark); Ar-Rahim refers to Allah's particular mercy directed especially towards believers (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims regard shirk as the most serious sin in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Possible points: Shirk directly contradicts Tawhid, which is the foundation of all Islamic belief — to associate a partner with Allah is to reject the most fundamental truth about God's nature (1+1 mark). The Qur'an teaches that shirk is an unforgivable sin for someone who dies unrepentant, making it uniquely serious among all human failings (1+1 mark). Shirk directs worship away from Allah to something less, which is both a profound injustice and a form of ingratitude for the blessings of creation (1+1 mark). Surah 112 (al-Ikhlas) affirms that Allah 'neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent' — any claim to the contrary is therefore a denial of this revealed truth (1+1 mark for citing a source). [6 marks: 3 marks per reason — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Tawhid makes it impossible for Muslims to respect other religious traditions.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Tawhid rules out polytheism as a form of shirk; the Christian Trinity is viewed as compromising Allah's oneness; Surah 112 directly addresses the claim that Allah 'begets' or has an equivalent; Islamic theology teaches that all previous religions were originally monotheistic but became corrupted — implying other traditions have deviated from truth. Arguments against: Islam teaches that Christians and Jews are 'People of the Book' who share prophets and scriptures with Muslims; the Qur'an calls for respectful dialogue; shirk is a theological category, not a personal moral judgement — Muslims can respect individuals while disagreeing with their beliefs; Islam teaches that all humans are born with the fitrah (natural inclination to monotheism), so other believers are not dismissed. Mastering: Both sides developed with named sources (Surah 112, Surah 53:19-25, 'People of the Book'), explicit weighing of theological disagreement vs practical respect, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with some sourcing; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or limited sourcing. Emerging: Brief, unsupported. [15 marks: SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State which Surah of the Qur'an is most directly associated with expressing the oneness of Allah.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes Tawhid?
options: The belief that Allah has 99 names
The absolute oneness of Allah, with no partners or equals
The mercy of Allah extended to all creation
The Shi'a doctrine of divinely appointed leaders

knowledge_checks.q: Surah 50:16 teaches that Allah is 'closer to him than his jugular vein.' Which attribute does this express?
Associating partners with Allah is called _____ and is considered the most serious sin in Islam.
Ar-Rahman refers to Allah's _____ mercy, extended to all of creation.
Match each name or term to its correct meaning:
right: Allah's particular mercy directed towards believers

flashcard_questions.a: The absolute oneness of Allah — no partner, equal or associate.
Associating partners with Allah; the most serious sin in Islam.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Surah expresses the oneness of Allah most directly?
What does Surah 50:16 teach about Allah?
flashcard_questions.a: That Allah is 'closer to him than his jugular vein' — expressing His immanence.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim?
flashcard_questions.a: Ar-Rahman = universal mercy (all creation); Ar-Rahim = particular mercy (for believers).

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Muslims regard the Christian Trinity as problematic?
flashcard_questions.a: Because associating Jesus with divine nature compromises Tawhid and is seen as shirk.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 112 say about Allah 'begetting'?
flashcard_questions.a: 'He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent.'

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'immanent' mean as an attribute of Allah?
flashcard_questions.a: That Allah is present and close to creation, aware of every individual.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'transcendent' mean as an attribute of Allah?
flashcard_questions.a: That Allah is beyond and above all creation, entirely unlike anything in the universe.

flashcard_questions.q: How do Shi'a Muslims argue that the Imamate does not compromise Tawhid?
flashcard_questions.a: The Imams are not divine; they are righteous human guides, not objects of worship.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah al-Baqarah (2:117) say about Allah's power?
flashcard_questions.a: That when He decrees something, He only says 'Be' and it is — expressing omnipotence.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Basmala, and which two names of Allah does it include?
flashcard_questions.a: The opening phrase 'In the name of Allah'; it includes Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim.

glossary_terms.definition: The 99 beautiful names of Allah that describe His attributes and qualities, used in worship and remembrance.
The central Islamic doctrine of the absolute oneness of Allah, affirming that God has no partner, equal or associate.
The Arabic term for associating partners with Allah, considered the most serious sin in Islam.
The worship of multiple gods or divine beings, which Muslims regard as the clearest form of shirk.
The Shi'a doctrine that religious and political leadership after the Prophet belonged to a line of divinely guided Imams from his family.
A quality of Allah meaning He is entirely beyond and above all creation, unlike anything in the universe.
A quality of Allah meaning He is present and intimately close to creation, aware of every individual.
